q.t: Which of these is a complete sentence?
q.e: Only this one tells us who (the baby) and what is said about it (is sleeping). The others leave you asking ‘what?’ or ‘who?’.

q.t: What kind of sentence is this? Where is my bag?
q.e: It asks a question and ends with a question mark.

q.t: What kind of sentence is this? Please open the door.
q.e: It makes a request. Orders, requests and advice are imperative.

q.t: What kind of sentence is this? What a beautiful garden!
q.e: It shows strong feeling (surprise, delight) and ends with !. It starts with ‘What’ but does not ask anything.

q.t: What kind of sentence is this? The earth goes round the sun.
q.e: It states a fact, so it is assertive (declarative).

q.t: Find the subject: My grandmother tells funny stories.
q.e: Ask ‘Who tells?’ → my grandmother. The rest (tells funny stories) is the predicate.

q.t: Find the predicate: The tall boy won the race.
q.e: The predicate is everything said about the subject (the tall boy): won the race.

q.t: Which punctuation mark ends an interrogative sentence?
q.e: A question always ends with a question mark.

q.t: Which is the negative form of She likes mangoes.?
q.e: No helping verb, so bring in ‘does’ to carry ‘not’. ‘does’ already shows the -s, so ‘likes’ goes back to ‘like’.

q.t: In Sit down., what is the hidden subject?
q.e: Every command is said to someone: (You) sit down. The subject ‘you’ is understood.

q.t: What kind of sentence is this? I wonder what she is cooking.
q.e: It states that I wonder — it does not ask the listener anything. So it is assertive and ends with a full stop.

q.t: Find the subject: Into the room rushed the excited children.
q.e: Ask ‘Who rushed?’ → the excited children. The subject can come after the verb.

q.t: Which sentence is correctly punctuated?
q.e: ‘How cold it is’ (subject before verb) is an exclamation. ‘How cold is it?’ (verb before subject) would be a question.

q.t: Change to a question: They have finished the work.
o: Do they have finished the work?
Did they have finished the work?
q.e: Move the helping verb ‘have’ before the subject. Do not add ‘do’ when a helping verb is already there.

q.t: Change to a question: He plays chess.
q.e: No helping verb, so bring in ‘does’. It carries the -s, so ‘plays’ becomes ‘play’.

q.t: Which of these is an imperative sentence?
q.e: ‘Never tell lies’ is advice/an order to ‘you’. The others state, ask or exclaim.

q.t: Find the predicate: The old clock on the wall stopped at midnight.
o: on the wall stopped at midnight
The old clock on the wall
q.e: Who stopped? The old clock on the wall (subject). What is said about it? stopped at midnight (predicate).

q.t: Which is the negative of We went to the zoo.?
o: We did not go to the zoo.
We did not went to the zoo.
We not went to the zoo.
We do not went to the zoo.
q.e: Bring in ‘did’ to carry ‘not’ and the past tense. Since ‘did’ already shows the past, ‘went’ goes back to ‘go’.

q.t: What kind of sentence is Help!?
q.e: It is a command — (You) help (me)! — said with strong feeling. One word can be a full sentence if the meaning is complete.

q.t: Which is NOT a sentence?
q.e: ‘Because it was raining’ leaves you asking ‘so what happened?’ It depends on another part to be complete.

q.t: What type of sentence is this? The phone rang, but nobody answered it.
q.e: Two complete sentences (The phone rang. Nobody answered it.) joined by ‘but’.

q.t: What type of sentence is this? I stayed home because I was ill.
q.e: ‘because I was ill’ cannot stand on its own; it depends on ‘I stayed home’. Main + dependent clause = complex.

q.t: What type of sentence is this? After lunch, the tired workers rested under the trees.
q.e: Only one subject–verb pair: workers rested. ‘After lunch’ and ‘under the trees’ are phrases, not clauses.

q.t: Choose the correct exclamatory form of It is a very brave act.
o: What a brave act it is!
How a brave act it is!
q.e: Use ‘What a …’ before a noun phrase (a brave act) and ‘How …’ before an adjective alone (How brave it is!).

q.t: Choose the correct exclamatory form of The view is very beautiful.
o: What a beautiful the view is!
q.e: ‘How + adjective + subject + verb!’ The subject comes before the verb in an exclamation.

q.t: Find the subject: Where have you kept my keys?
q.e: Turn it into a statement: You have kept my keys (somewhere). Who has kept them? → you.

q.t: Which sentence is assertive?
q.e: It states a fact (even though it is negative in meaning). A negative statement is still assertive.

q.t: Join into a compound sentence: Hurry up. You will miss the bus.
o: Hurry up, or you will miss the bus.
Hurry up and you will miss the bus.
Hurry up, but you will miss the bus.
Hurry up, so you will miss the bus.
q.e: ‘or’ shows the other choice: either you hurry, or you miss the bus. ‘and’ would mean hurrying causes missing it.

q.t: Change to a negative without changing meaning: Everyone was present.
q.e: If everyone was present, then no one was absent. Two ‘negatives’ (no + absent) keep the meaning positive.

q.t: Which of these questions is correctly formed?
q.e: Question word + did + subject + base verb. ‘did’ carries the past tense, so ‘left’ becomes ‘leave’.

q.t: Find the complete subject: The book that you lent me last week is very interesting.
o: The book that you lent me last week
The book that you lent me
q.e: What is interesting? The book that you lent me last week. The ‘that …’ part describes ‘the book’, so it belongs to the subject.

q.t: What type of sentence is this? When the rain stopped, the children went out and played football.
q.e: ‘When the rain stopped’ cannot stand alone — it depends on the main part. (The main part has two verbs sharing one subject, but the dependent clause is what makes it complex.)

q.t: Which sentence ends with the WRONG mark?
o: Can you tell me where the station is.
Tell me where the station is.
I asked him where the station was.
q.e: ‘Can you tell me …’ asks a question (it begins with the helping verb ‘can’), so it needs ‘?’. The other two statements contain a question word but ask nothing.

q.t: Change to assertive: Who does not love his country?
o: Some people do not love their country.
q.e: This is a question that expects no answer (a rhetorical question). ‘Who does not …?’ really means ‘there is no one who does not …’, i.e. everyone does.

q.t: Change to assertive: What a fool I have been!
o: I have been a great fool.
I have not been a fool.
q.e: An exclamation of ‘What a …!’ shows a strong degree, so the statement uses ‘very’ or ‘great’.

q.t: Combine into a complex sentence: He was tired. He kept walking.
o: Although he was tired, he kept walking.
He was tired and he kept walking.
He was tired, so he kept walking.
He was tired or he kept walking.
q.e: ‘Although’ turns one part into a dependent clause and shows the contrast (tired, yet walking). ‘and’/‘so’ make a compound sentence or the wrong meaning.

q.t: Which sentence has the subject placed AFTER the verb?
q.e: Who comes? the bus — it comes after ‘comes’. In ‘Is the bus here?’ only the helping verb moves; the subject still comes before ‘here’.

q.t: Change to imperative: You should not waste water.
o: Water should not be wasted by you.
q.e: An imperative drops the ‘you’ and starts with the verb. For a negative order use ‘Do not’ / ‘Don’t’.

q.t: How many clauses (subject–verb groups) are in: I know that she will come if you call her.
q.e: I know | that she will come | if you call her — three subjects with their own verbs: I know, she will come, you call.

q.t: Change to a negative question with the same meaning: She is very clever.
o: Is she not clever at all?
q.e: ‘Isn't she …?’ expects the answer ‘yes’, so it keeps the positive meaning. A plain ‘Is she …?’ is a real question with no expected answer.
